title: Hackers Put Apple and Tesla Trade Secrets on the Dark Web. The Leak Came From a Tata Plant in Tamil Nadu.
excerpt: A ransomware crew claims to have lifted iPhone inspection manuals and Tesla part drawings from Tata Electronics, the company carrying India's bet that it can build the West's gadgets. The breach lands as India races to become Apple's factory floor.
body:
India wants the world to trust it with the West's most valuable hardware. A breach at Tata Electronics, disclosed this week, is the first serious test of that trust.

A ransomware group operating a dark-web leak site called World Leaks has published files it claims were stolen from **Tata Electronics**, the Tata Group arm that assembles iPhones in India. According to a Reuters review, the dump includes a 52-page document bearing Apple's proprietary markings that details quality-inspection standards for iPhone circuit boards, along with files and folders referencing "Hosur" — the Tamil Nadu town where Tata runs its main iPhone assembly plant. A search of the database for "Apple" reportedly returned 181 files; one folder, labelled "NV36 Chargeport Controller – North America," and drawings tied to a Tesla project codenamed "Highland" suggest carmaker secrets were swept up too.

Tata has informed some employees at its iPhone operations of the breach. The data has apparently been sitting on the dark web since at least June 10th. Apple and Tesla did not comment.

### Why this is bigger than one factory

Tata Electronics is not a peripheral supplier. It accounts for roughly a third of Apple's iPhone production in India, with Foxconn making the rest. And India's share of global iPhone output has gone vertical — from about 6% four years ago to a projected **26% in 2026**, according to Counterpoint Research. Tim Cook has said the majority of iPhones sold in the United States will soon carry a "Made in India" tag. The entire premise of Apple's "China+1" strategy is that India can be a manufacturing base that is not just cheaper but *safer* than a China increasingly entangled in trade war.

A leak of Apple's confidential inspection standards punctures part of that pitch. The bill of materials and tolerances in those documents are the kind of process knowledge rivals and counterfeiters covet. More damaging than any single file is the signal: the crown-jewel supply chain that Apple is moving to India is only as secure as the cybersecurity maturity of its Indian partners.

### The diaspora angle: trust is the product

For the millions of NRIs who buy Apple and Tesla products, the immediate risk is low — this is intellectual property, not customer data. But the strategic stake is high and personal. The story the diaspora has been telling itself, and the world, is that India is graduating from back-office and call-center work to building the planet's most advanced consumer hardware. That graduation depends on Western firms believing Indian factories can guard their secrets as well as Taiwanese or Japanese ones can.

There is a cruel irony here. India produces a large share of the world's cybersecurity workforce; Indian-origin engineers run security at some of the biggest American tech firms, and Indian cyber startups are raising rounds at a healthy clip. Yet the breach landed on home soil, at a marquee national champion. For Indian security professionals abroad, it is both a reputational dent and a market opening — the manufacturing build-out India is chasing will need exactly the operational-technology security expertise the diaspora has in abundance.

### What comes next

Expect Apple to tighten supplier security audits across its India footprint, and expect Tata to face uncomfortable questions about how long the data was exposed before anyone noticed. CERT-In, India's computer emergency response team, has been pushing tougher breach-disclosure timelines; this is the kind of high-profile incident that tends to accelerate enforcement.

The deeper lesson for India's ambitions is unglamorous but decisive. Winning the world's manufacturing means inheriting the world's threat model. The factories are going up fast. The security culture around them will have to catch up faster — because in a globalized supply chain, a leak in Hosur is felt in Cupertino, and the diaspora's bragging rights ride on which one the world remembers.
